title: Orpheus and Eurydice
text:
Orpheus, the finest singer and lyre player who ever lived, married Eurydice. Soon after the wedding, as she walked in a meadow, she was bitten on the ankle by a snake and died.

Orpheus mourned her above ground until he could bear it no longer. Then he did what no living man should do: he went down through the gate of the underworld, past the ghosts of the dead, and stood before Hades and Persephone. He played his lyre and sang. He asked only that Eurydice be given back to him for the span of a natural life; she would come back to them in time anyway. His song was so moving that the ghosts wept, Tantalus forgot his thirst, and for the first time, it was said, the cheeks of the Furies were wet with tears.

The rulers of the dead could not refuse. Eurydice could go, on one condition: Orpheus must not look back at her until they had left the underworld.

They climbed the steep, dark, silent path. They were almost at the edge of the upper world when Orpheus, afraid she might be faltering and longing to see her, turned around. At once she slipped back. She reached out to him, and he to her, but he caught only the air. She did not reproach him, Ovid says; what could she complain of, except that she had been loved? With a faint farewell, she was gone.
lesson: Love can attempt almost anything, but grief eventually asks us to trust and let go. Holding on too tightly can lose what we are trying to keep.
location: Thrace (Greek myth); written in Rome, Italy
source: Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 10; Virgil, Georgics, Book 4
